1.title: Evidence of Charge
1.text:
Evidence of Charge

Electrostatics is the study of electric charges that can be collected and held in one place.

Our big question for this lesson: why does shuffling your shoes across a carpet give you a shock when you touch a metal doorknob? That little zap is static electricity. In this module, we'll explore electrostatics, the study of electric charges that can be collected and held in one place.

Static electricity shows up at every scale, from giant bolts of lightning down to electrons nudging each other inside atoms. Later, you'll study electric current, which is the net movement of electric charge. For now, our charges are staying put.

2.title: The Electrostatic Force
2.text:
The Electrostatic Force

The electrostatic force is the force between charged objects; it can beat gravity and it fades as charge leaks away.

On a dry day, have you noticed your hair reaching for your comb? Or socks clinging together out of the dryer? Pull off a wool hat, like in Figure 1, and your hair stands up. Something must be pulling up on that hair harder than gravity pulls it down. The hat exerts an electrostatic force on the hair that's greater than Earth's gravitational force.

These two forces behave differently, though. Hair is attracted to the hat only after the hat has rubbed it, and if you wait, the attraction fades. Gravity needs no rubbing, and it never fades.

Why does this happen more on dry days? Moist air and the thin film of water it leaves on surfaces let charge leak away quickly. In dry air, charge stays put longer, so your hair keeps standing up.

testIt.how: Set the humidity, then tap to rub the hat on your hair.

3.title: Your Investigation Toolkit
3.text:
Your Investigation Toolkit

Collect evidence in your Science Journal and investigate with activities.

Use your Science Journal to record the evidence you collect as you work through the readings and activities in this lesson.

Online, the Forensics Lab called Static Charge lets you investigate how static electric charges affect each other and neutral objects. And as you go, ask yourself: what information from this lesson can help you answer the Unit and Module questions?

4.title: Investigating Charge with Tape, Like Charges
4.text:
Investigating Charge with Tape, Like Charges

Objects with like charges always repel each other.

You can explore charge with plain transparent tape. Fold over about 5 millimeters at the end of a 10-centimeter strip to make a handle. Stick it to a dry, smooth surface like a desk, then stick a second, similar strip next to it.

Now quickly pull both strips off and bring them near each other. They push apart! Pulling them off the desk gave them electric charge. Since the strips were prepared the same way, they have the same kind of charge. Two objects with like charges always repel each other.

testIt.name: Tape strips
testIt.how: Tap to peel two strips off the desk and bring them together.

5.title: Unlike Charges
5.text:
Unlike Charges

There is a second type of charge, and unlike charges attract.

Now stick one strip on the desk and put the second strip right on top of it. Use the bottom strip's handle to slowly pull both off together. Rub them with your fingers until they're no longer attracted to you; that removes their charge.

Next, hold one handle in each hand and quickly pull the strips apart. They're charged again, since they're attracted to your hands. Bring them close together, and this time they attract each other! Because they attract, they can't have the same charge. So there's a second type of charge, and unlike charges attract.

testIt.name: B and T
testIt.how: Tap to step through stacking, discharging, and splitting the strips.

6.title: Testing Other Objects
6.text:
Testing Other Objects

A charged object attracts one tape strip and repels the other when the strips have different charges.

Let's use the tape to test other objects. Rub a plastic comb on your clothes and set it on the desk. Prepare your tape pair again, labeling the handle of the bottom strip B and the top strip T. Pull them off together, discharge them, then pull them apart.

Hold the strips, one in each hand, and bring each one near the comb. One strip is attracted, and the other is repelled. Figure 2 shows all three tests. Try it again with glass, silk, or wool.

How could you tell which strip is positive? Charge a material known to go positive, like glass rubbed with silk, and see which strip it repels. The strip it repels has the same positive charge.

testIt.name: Test objects
testIt.how: Tap to bring the next object near strips B and T.

7.title: Types of Charge
7.text:
Types of Charge

There are two types of charge, positive and negative; rubbing materials together separates them.

Your tape experiments show there are only two types of charge. Benjamin Franklin named them positive and negative. Ordinary matter contains both.

Materials differ in how easily they pick up charge. Hard rubber and plastic tend to become negatively charged. Glass and wool tend to become positively charged. Rubbing two materials together separates the two types of charge. So a plastic pen rubbed on your clothes, like the one at the start of the module, would most likely end up negatively charged. To see why, let's zoom in to the microscopic level.

8.title: A Microscopic View of Charge
8.text:
A Microscopic View of Charge

A neutral object has exactly equal amounts of positive and negative charge.

Electric charges live inside atoms. In 1897, J. J. Thomson discovered that all materials contain low-mass, negatively charged particles called electrons. Between 1909 and 1911, Ernest Rutherford, who had earlier worked with Thomson, found that an atom has a massive, positively charged nucleus surrounded by a cloud of electrons.

From these and many other experiments, we know atoms are normally neutral. In science, neutral means an exact balance: the negative charge exactly cancels the positive charge, so there's no net charge. In everyday speech, neutral means not taking sides, the way Switzerland has historically been a neutral country.

testIt.how: Add or remove electrons from a neutral atom with 6 protons.

9.title: Transfer and Separation of Charge
9.text:
Transfer and Separation of Charge

Charging is the transfer of electrons; charge is conserved, never created or destroyed.

With a little added energy, an atom's outer electrons can be pulled away. An atom missing electrons has a net positive charge. The freed electrons can stay loose or attach to other atoms, giving those atoms a net negative charge. So, on the microscopic level, getting charged means transferring electrons.

Here's our focus question in action. When you rub rubber shoes on a wool rug, the energy of rubbing knocks outer electrons off atoms in the wool, and they move to your shoes, as in Figure 3. The shoes end up with extra electrons and a net negative charge, and the rug, missing electrons, has a net positive charge. Your body now carries extra charge, and when your hand nears a metal doorknob, it jumps across in a spark. That's your shock!

The total charge of shoes plus rug stays the same. Charge is conserved, meaning individual charges are never created or destroyed. A net positive or negative charge simply means electrons have moved.

testIt.name: Rug
testIt.how: Shuffle across the rug: electrons move from rug to shoes.

10.title: Effects of Separation of Charge
10.text:
Effects of Separation of Charge

In everyday charging, charges are not created; they are separated.

Separation of charge is all around us. Processes inside a thundercloud can leave the bottom of the cloud negatively charged and the top positively charged. Charge can move from a road onto a car driving over it. Even an MP3 player rubbing in your pocket can charge your earbuds enough to give you a little shock.

In every one of these cases, charges aren't created. They're separated.

testIt.how: Slide time as charge separates in the cloud.

11.title: Conductors and Insulators
11.text:
Conductors and Insulators

An electric insulator is a material through which charge will not move easily; an electric conductor lets charges move about easily.

Hold a plastic rod or comb at its middle and rub one end on your clothes. Only the rubbed end gets charged. The electrons that moved onto the plastic stayed right where they landed. A material through which charge won't move easily is an electric insulator. Your tape strips were insulators too, since their charge stayed put. Glass, dry wood, most plastics, cloth, and dry air are all good insulators.

Now set a metal rod on an insulating support, so it's completely surrounded by insulator. Touch a charged comb to one end, and the charge spreads over the whole rod almost instantly. A material that lets charges move about easily is an electric conductor. Electrons move through the metal and carry the charge with them. Figure 4 compares the two.

That's why electrical wires are coated with rubber: the metal inside conducts charge where we want it, and the rubber insulator keeps that charge from reaching your hand.

testIt.how: Tap to touch the charged comb to the other rod.

12.title: Metals and Air as Conductors
12.text:
Metals and Air as Conductors

Air becomes a conductor when strong forces strip electrons from its molecules, forming a plasma.

Most metals are good conductors, because at least one electron per atom comes loose easily. Those electrons don't belong to any one atom; they roam through the whole metal. Copper and aluminum are excellent conductors used to carry charge commercially. Some nonmetals conduct well too, like graphite and plasma, which is a mix of negative electrons and positive ions.

Air is normally an insulator, but sometimes charges move through it as if it were a conductor. The spark between your finger and a doorknob discharges you; the excess charge leaves your body, and you're neutral again. Lightning does the same for a thundercloud. For that brief moment, air conducts.

How? A spark needs freely moving charged particles in air, which is normally neutral. In lightning, the excess charges in the cloud and on the ground exert enough force to tear electrons off air molecules for a moment. The electrons and positive ions form a plasma, and plasma conducts.

testIt.how: Build up the field between cloud and ground.

13.title: Real-World Physics, Conductor or Insulator?
13.text:
Real-World Physics, Conductor or Insulator?

The same element can be a conductor or an insulator depending on how its atoms are bonded.

It's tempting to sort every element into conductor or insulator, but the form an element takes can change the answer. Carbon is a great example.

As diamond, carbon is an insulator. As graphite, carbon conducts. The difference is in how the carbon atoms bond. Graphite's bonds let some electrons move around, so graphite is a much better conductor than diamond, even though both are made of nothing but carbon atoms.
